analysis.one_liner: Lets investors lower capital gains taxes by adjusting purchase prices upward for inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would cut capital gains taxes for people who hold stocks, crypto, or business property for more than three years, was introduced by three Republican senators and never advanced past a committee referral before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let non-corporate taxpayers who sell stocks, digital assets, or business property they held for more than three years increase the purchase price the tax code uses to calculate their gain — adjusted upward for inflation measured by the GDP deflator [S2][S3]. A bigger purchase price means a smaller taxable gain and a smaller capital gains tax bill [S3]. The bill includes special pass-through rules so mutual fund, REIT, partnership, and S corporation investors get the same adjustment [S2][S3]. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received any further action [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Investors who sell appreciated assets they have held for more than three years: holders of common stock, cryptocurrency and other digital assets, and tangible business or investment property [S2][S3]. The bill covers only assets acquired after December 31, 2023, and requires written documentation of the original purchase price [S3]. The benefit scales with the size of the gain, so it is worth the most to people with large, long-held appreciated positions — and it extends to investors through mutual funds, REITs, partnerships, and S corporations [S3]. Corporations are explicitly excluded, but wealthy individuals and family businesses are the core beneficiaries [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Allows a taxpayer (other than a corporation) who sells an asset held more than three years to substitute an inflation-adjusted purchase price for the original one, shrinking the taxable gain on stocks, digital assets, and tangible property [S2][S3].

Extends the same inflation adjustment through regulated investment companies, REITs, partnerships, S corporations, and common trust funds, so ordinary fund and trust investors as well as business partners receive the benefit [S2][S3].

Includes guardrails: the adjustment applies only with written documentation of the original purchase price, holding periods are suspended when risk is hedged, and the IRS may disallow adjustments engineered through transfers between people for the principal purpose of increasing them [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, and ultimately everyone who relies on federal programs or would otherwise share the burden of federal revenue. Every dollar of gain the bill removes from the tax base is a dollar of capital gains tax not collected, and since the largest long-held gains are concentrated among the wealthiest households, the foregone revenue would come disproportionately from taxes those households currently pay. Wage earners who rent, hold their savings in retirement accounts, or sell few appreciated assets get essentially nothing from the bill but share in covering the revenue loss.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers who don't hold appreciated assets

drawbacks.text: The tax cut only helps people who own appreciated stocks, crypto, or business property they hold over three years and sell at a gain — a group concentrated among higher-income households. Renters, wage earners, and people whose savings sit in retirement accounts get no benefit but bear the revenue loss through taxes, borrowing, or program cuts.

By shrinking the capital gains base on long-held assets, the bill reduces federal revenue at a time when the tax code already taxes long-term capital gains at lower rates than wages; the bill text contains no offsetting revenue increase.

The rules are complex — special formulas for funds and REITs, short-sale rules, related-party limits, and anti-abuse authority for the IRS — adding compliance and administrative burden for a benefit most taxpayers would never use [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrowly distributed: inflation genuinely erodes the value of long-held investments, and adjusting for it is a defensible principle that some economists support. But this bill would deliver the entire benefit to households with large, long-held appreciated assets while the cost — foregone federal revenue — spreads across everyone. The people most likely to hold a stock or crypto position for over three years outside a retirement account are exactly the people least likely to need tax relief. On balance, the bill is a targeted tax cut for asset-rich households dressed in a fair-sounding inflation-fix frame.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Ted Cruz introduced the bill on April 20, 2023, with Senators Mike Braun and Bill Hagerty as the only cosponsors [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance [S5].
The action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — through the end of the 118th Congress in January 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal taxpayers as a whole: the revenue the bill would have foregone — concentrated among taxes paid by wealthy asset holders — stays in the Treasury. The bill's three sponsors gained nothing from it passing nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal taxpayers; the bill's sponsors gained nothing

for.name: Sen. Ted Cruz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and drafted the inflation-indexing language for long-held stocks, digital assets, and business property

for.name: Sens. Mike Braun and Bill Hagerty

against.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee action after its referral, leaving it to die in committee

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Republicans; the bill drew no Democratic cosponsors and never moved in the Senate Finance Committee, where the Democratic caucus held the majority.

industries.note: The bill writes detailed pass-through formulas so fund and REIT investors capture the inflation adjustment on the funds' holdings [S3]. That would make long-term fund investing more tax-favored, with the revenue cost spread across all taxpayers [S2].
Digital assets recorded on a distributed ledger are explicitly named as indexable assets, so long-term crypto sellers would owe tax on less of their gain [S3].

industries.industry: Private equity, real estate, and family business owners
industries.note: Partnership, S corporation, and tangible property rules extend the adjustment to business and real estate sellers held over three years, cutting their tax on exit [S3].
